title: Andrew M. Byrd
text:
About Me
My research is about finding new ways to solve hard problems in historical linguistics, more and more often with computers. I especially work on Proto-Indo-European (PIE), the reconstructed ancestor of most of the languages of Europe, Iran, and northern India.
I also try to bring PIE to the public, through constructed languages for games and TV, translations, and interviews.

What I Work On

A searchable database of PIE roots, built from several etymological dictionaries.


Immersive PIE
With Brenna Byrd: a textbook and four novellas that teach PIE through stories.


Conlangs
Languages for games like Far Cry Primal and Flintlock: The Siege of Dawn.

title: Research
text:
Question: Which sounds begin the roots of Proto-Indo-European? Is b really as rare as the handbooks say?
Data: Julius Pokorny’s Indogermanisches etymologisches Wörterbuch (1959), the standard 20th-century dictionary of PIE roots, from its online edition. I cleaned it into a table of 2,077 roots with Python and pandas.
Preliminary results: I found the first sound of every root, and counted how many roots begin with each of the fifteen stops:



Place
Voiceless
Voiced
Voiced aspirated




Labial
p 133
b 28
bh 130


Dental
t 108
d 57
dh 67


Palatal
k̂ 92
ĝ 22
ĝh 44


Velar
k 187
g 50
gh 57


Labiovelar
kʷ 24
gʷ 36
gʷh 12



Only 28 roots begin with b, under a quarter as many as begin with p or bh. At every other place, the voiced stop has at least half as many roots as the aspirate. The gap at the lips is real.

Most of the 28 b-roots aren’t ordinary words at all: they mean things like ‘to bleat’, ‘babble’, and ‘sound of barking’. Sound-symbolic words often break the normal rules.
